To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) prenatal and postnatal stressors, as well as maternal anxiety and depression during pregnancy, are associated with increased asthma risk in the offspring; (2) these associations may be mediated through altered regulation of the SAM system and HPA axis, as evidenced by the associations between maternal stress, maternal cortisol and/or SAM activity during pregnancy and asthma outcomes in the offspring; and (3) the association between prenatal stress and asthma may be stronger among children who have a family history of asthma
prenatal maternal stress and poor caregiving in infancy are associated with altered neuroimmune responses and asthma risk in childhood.
prenatal maternal stress and poor early-life parenting practices are associated with altered neuroimmune regulation and increased risk for asthma and allergy expression in the offspring.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the biological mechanisms by which stress and other psychosocial factors influence asthma risk.
identifying the mechanisms by which psychological factors influence asthma risk.
the role of stress in childhood asthma risk and the mechanisms underlying the relationship between stress and asthma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stress is a risk factor for the development of childhood asthma.

the evidence linking prenatal stress and early life adversity to asthma risk is strong, although it is not yet possible to draw conclusions regarding the relative contribution of each factor to asthma development.
stress and childhood asthma risk are related and the evidence is compelling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stress response systems (eg, HPA and SAM) are important mediators of the effects of stress on the development of asthma, but that they do not work in isolation.
maternal stress, especially during the third trimester of pregnancy, and early life caregiving experiences can have long-term consequences for the regulation of the HPA and SAM axes.
maternal stress and early-life caregiving experiences can have profound effects on the developing child, with consequences that may be expressed in later life as asthma and allergy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stress response systems are not only activated during the stressor but also remain in a state of increased reactivity, even after the stressor has passed.
the stress response is a key biological mechanism that links early-life adversity with asthma risk and may also contribute to the development of other immune-mediated diseases.
there is a need for a more comprehensive understanding of the role of psychological factors in the etiology and expression of asthma.
